_about: Hand-kept input of the proof map (build.py). Everything else on the map is read from the paper's LaTeX, the PDF (numbering check), lean/README.md and the Lean sources. 'labels' are short names for results the paper leaves untitled, shown in the graph only. 'lean_part' says what part of a result the Lean formalisation covers, where it covers only part (from lean/README.md, 'What it does not show'); 'lean_related', for a result it does not formalise, a related fact that it does prove. 'passages' lists the passages of the paper's running text that the site shows (see its own '_about'). 'notes' are short AI-generated reading aids, shown labelled as such. 'off_graph' lists results kept off the graph, with the reason shown under it ({label} becomes a link). 'route' gives each step of the route (the same ten steps as the public site's Prove page, step n following section n of the paper, whose results are listed in 'prove_steps') a title and a one-sentence summary; the summaries are AI-generated and are labelled as a paraphrase where they appear.

lean_part.comp:base: On the nine level-1 supertiles computed by exact.py, taken as input: their geometry, and that $A$ is $v_0$ of the first tile of the Mystic (the paper's definition of $A$ at level 1), are not checked; the Lean has no Mystic.
lean_part.lem:gap: In combinatorial form: every edge of $N_b$ is glued in $N_{b+2}$ (part (b)), and every vertex of every tile of $N_b$ is surrounded by tiles of $N_{b+2}$ (part (a) at the vertices of tiles). The step from tile vertices to points of the plane is part of assumption (M3).
lean_part.thm:A: In combinatorial form: for any chain of supertiles whose union has every edge glued; the nest is one. That a tiling whose hierarchy covers the plane is such a union is assumption (M2).
lean_part.thm:B: In combinatorial form: for the union of the blocks $N_b$. That this union is the nest tiling of the plane is Prop 8.2 and Prop 8.4, which are geometric and not formalised (assumption (M3)); Lemma 8.3(a), which Prop 8.4 uses, is formalised at the vertices of tiles.
lean_part.lem:box: For the patches with the signature, the only ones the proof uses: following the ribbon pairs their rim ports without fixed points. The box of a general patch is not formalised.
lean_part.lem:gluing: In the two forms the proof uses: for compositions, glued from boxes, and for supertiles glued from their children.

lean_related.prop:pattern: For the supertiles it builds from the tables, the Lean proves that the parent's rim, read from Table 3, is the rim of the glued children (`Statement.rim_edgeAt`, `Statement.own_rot`, `Statement.parent_vtx`): step (v) of the Reduction in Section 7.1. That actual supertiles are glued as the tables say is this proposition, part of assumption (M1).

passages._about: Passages of the paper's running text, between its numbered items, that its proofs cite or whose terms its statements use, so that the site shows what every statement and proof on it rests on. Each is found by the exact start of its first paragraph ('start') and runs for 'paras' paragraphs (default 1). It is shown in full on its step's page, where it has the address #psg-<key>, and on the pages of the results whose proofs cite it ('cited_by') or that it follows ('follows'); the results whose statements use its terms ('terms_for') link to it by 'term'. Titles and terms are plain text. The build stops if a start is not in the paper exactly once.

notes.lem:zigzag: Where two neighbouring supertiles share a stretch of rim with hooks at every inner vertex, the ribbon zigzags along it: it crosses at every edge and turns back at every vertex, alternately on each side. So which end each connection reaches depends only on whether the stretch has an even or odd number of edges. This is what lets Lemma 7.1 lengthen glued sides by two edges without changing how anything joins.
notes.comp:compose: This is the one finite check behind the induction step of the Signature Theorem; its base is Computation 7.5. For each of the nine kinds and both signs, the composition is built from Tables 1 to 4 and the level-1 lengths $\ell_1$ and $d_1$ alone, and the ribbon is followed from every port. No geometry enters. Lemmas 7.1 and 7.2 carry the result to every level (Proposition 7.4).
notes.lem:gap: Each block of the nest touches its parent's rim only along its own side 2, and that side lies strictly inside the parent's side 4, away from the ends of side 4. So the block lies strictly inside the block two levels up. Part (a) makes the blocks fill the plane (Proposition 8.4); part (b) says every edge of a block is glued two levels up. The Lean proves (b), and (a) at the vertices of tiles.
notes.thm:B: The proof puts three things together. Lemma 3.4: every strand is a cycle or a two-way infinite path. No strand is a cycle, by the Signature Theorem (argued after Proposition 8.4). And the strand graph is connected: any two pieces lie in some block $N_b$ (Proposition 8.4), whose arcs all lie on one arc of $N_{b+4}$ (Theorem 9.1).
notes.thm:A: Any closed strand would be made of finitely many pieces, so it would lie inside one supertile, and by the Signature Theorem no supertile contains one. The hypothesis that the hierarchy covers the plane is what puts every tile, and so every finite set of pieces, inside a single supertile. Lemma 3.4 then turns "no cycles" into "every strand is a two-way infinite path".
notes.thm:smkgs: This is the input from the spectre paper: tiles group uniquely into supertiles, level after level, and at each level the supertiles fit together like marked hexagons, mirrored on alternate levels. Nothing here is proved in this paper; everything about supertiles further on rests on it.
notes.prop:pattern: This turns the spectre paper's hexagon pictures into tables: which kinds the children are (Table 1), which sides are glued to which (Table 2), and how the parent's sides and its crossover corner are made from the children's (Table 3). Because the same tables hold at every level, the rest of the proof can treat any level by the same finite bookkeeping. In the Lean, these tables are data, and that real supertiles follow them is assumption (M1).
notes.lem:rigid: Two supertiles of the same kind and level are copies of each other, by exactly one rotation and translation that also lines up all their descendants. The proof is an induction from the Mystic, which has no symmetry. It makes the side lengths $\ell_m$ well defined (Section 6), carries Computation 7.5 from the nine drawn clusters to every level-1 supertile, and shows that the blocks of the nest do not depend on the choices made in building them (Proposition 8.2).
notes.lem:degree2: Each ribbon piece has two ends, and each end meets exactly one piece of the neighbouring tile. So the pieces form a graph in which every vertex has degree 2, and such a graph is a union of cycles and two-way infinite paths. Theorems A and B both start from this.
notes.lem:box: Seen from outside, a patch of tiles is just a pairing of the ports on its rim; the pieces that no rim port reaches form its closed strands. This “box”, and whether the patch has a closed strand, is all that later sections need to know about a patch.
notes.lem:gluing: The box of a patch glued from smaller patches can be worked out from their boxes alone: alternate between the small boxes' pairings and the straight-through rule across shared edges. This is what lets the proof compute with supertiles as black boxes instead of tile by tile.
notes.lem:tilesig: A single tile has the signature by the design itself: the one crossing sits at its vertices $v_0$ and $v_1$, and every other vertex is a hook.
notes.prop:letters: The length of a supertile's side depends only on a letter (one of eight) carried by that side, and the eight lengths obey one linear recurrence from level to level. So side lengths at every level are known exactly from the level-1 counts.
notes.prop:fib: Solving the recurrence of Proposition 6.1: every side length is a Fibonacci number, twice one, or one plus or minus 2. The proof is a direct substitution.
notes.cor:parity: Read off the Fibonacci forms: each side length is odd at every level or even at every level. By the Zigzag Lemma only parities of shared runs matter, so this fixed pattern of parities is the heart of why one computation covers all levels.
notes.lem:Apos: Where the crossover corner sits: at vertex 0 for eight of the nine kinds, and part-way along side 5 for $\Sigma$, at a distance that is again a Fibonacci expression and always even.
notes.lem:bounds: Every side is at least 5 edges long and the $\Sigma$ corner is at least 6 and 4 edges from the ends of its side. These margins make sure a lengthening move can always be placed away from the ends of sides and from the $\Sigma$ corner.
notes.lem:lengthen: Lengthening a glued pair of sides by two edges cuts one edge into three. By the Zigzag Lemma, a path of 3 edges joins its ends exactly as a path of 1 edge does, and the two new vertices are hooks. So the move changes nothing about how the ports of the composition are paired, and the signature survives. A move on a side that lies on the rim just adds two rim vertices, both hooks.
notes.lem:reach: The side lengths at any level can be reached from the level-1 lengths by such two-edge moves, through compositions that are all well defined. Lengths only grow and never change parity, so this is possible; the proof picks each move with care so that it stays away from the ends of sides and from the $\Sigma$ corner. So a property that holds at the level-1 lengths and survives every move holds at every level.
notes.prop:compose: Three ingredients make the induction: the 18 compositions at level-1 lengths have the signature (Computation 7.3), each move keeps it (Lemma 7.1), and every level is reached by moves (Lemma 7.2). So the compositions at every level have the signature.
notes.comp:base: The level-1 supertiles, built tile by tile from the actual geometry in exact arithmetic, have the signature, with the crossover corner at vertex 0, or for $\Sigma$ six edges along side 5 (the case $m=1$ of Lemma 6.4). This is the base of the induction in Theorem 7.6, and it also fixes the starting lengths $\ell_1$ and $d_1$.
notes.thm:signature: Every supertile, at every level, looks the same from outside: a hook at every rim vertex except two adjacent ones, which carry the crossover, and no closed strand inside. The induction goes level by level: if the children have the signature, the parent is glued as a composition, and Proposition 7.4 says that composition has it.
notes.con:nest: How the nest is built: take a $\Delta$ supertile of some level, follow child 1 down to a single tile, and move everything so that tile sits in a fixed place. Doing this for larger and larger levels grows the nest outwards from that one tile.
notes.prop:nestwell: The blocks $N_b$ come out the same however large the starting supertile and whatever choices were made, by rigidity (Lemma 2.6). So the nest is well defined, and each block is child 1 of the next.
notes.prop:nesttiling: The blocks of the nest cover the whole plane with no overlaps. The proof grows outwards: by the Grandparent Lemma, any tile touching a block lies in the block two levels up, so every tile within a bounded distance is eventually included.
notes.thm:merge: Following every arc of a block up the nest, a few levels at a time. By the junction map each arc of $N_b$ lands on a junction hook of the next block (four of the five junctions occur for $b$ even, three for $b$ odd) or, along side 2 of $N_b$, on a hook of the next block itself; all of these lie well inside sides, so the map applies to them again one level up. After three levels ($b$ even) or four ($b$ odd), every arc of $N_b$ is on the single hook at junction 12. These bounds are exact: one level fewer leaves two arcs.
notes.comp:junction: The level-1 version of the junction map. In the composition of a $\Delta$ from its eight children at the level-1 lengths, built from the tables alone, every arc of child 1, except the hooks strictly inside its side 2 (which lie on the parent's rim already), ends on the hook at one of the junctions that Table 6 names, depending mostly only on which side of child 1 it leaves from. Like Computation 7.3, it is checked port by port, by a program and by Lean's kernel.
notes.lem:junctionmap: The junction map holds at every level, not just at level-1 lengths: the same two-edge moves that carry the signature (Lemmas 7.1 and 7.2) also carry this property, provided the cuts stay at least two edges from the ends of child 1's sides.
notes.lem:junctions: Bookkeeping from Table 3: the five junctions, and the inside of the small block's side 2, all lie well inside sides of the bigger block, at least two edges from the ends. That margin is what lets the junction map be applied again one level up.

prove_steps._about: Which results of the paper each of the ten steps of the public site's Prove page (and of this site's Route) is made of, in this order; step n follows section n of the paper, and step 1, the introduction, has no results of its own. Every label here is named in its step's text on the Prove page (SPECTRE_KNOT_DEV's site build checks it).

1.title: The setting, the two theorems and the method
1.summary: Every tile carries the same decoration, fourteen ribbon pieces with one crossing; the Daedalus Theorem says that no strand closes in any tiling whose supertile hierarchy covers the plane, the Ariadne Theorem that the nest tiling has a single strand, and the proof rests on three ideas, black boxes, zigzags and fixed parities, with merging up the nest for the Ariadne Theorem.

2.title: Spectre tilings and their supertiles
2.summary: Every homochiral tiling by $\Tile$ groups uniquely into supertiles of nine kinds, level above level, and every level is assembled by the same tables (cited from the spectre paper); two supertiles of the same kind and level are copies of each other.

3.title: The decoration and its strands
3.summary: Every tile carries the same fourteen ribbon pieces and ribbons run straight through each edge, so every strand is a closed loop or a two-way infinite path.

4.title: Boxes and the signature
4.summary: Seen from outside, a patch is a box, a pairing of the ports on its rim, and boxes glue by following ports; the signature is a hook at every rim vertex but two adjacent ones, where the ribbons cross over, and no closed strand inside, and a tile has it.

5.title: The Zigzag Lemma
5.summary: Where two boxes with hooks are glued along a path, the ribbons zigzag along it and come out according to the parity of its length alone, so lengthening a shared path by two edges changes nothing.

6.title: Side lengths
6.summary: Side lengths depend only on their letters and are Fibonacci forms that only grow and never change parity; the crossover corner is vertex 0, or for $\Sigma$ an even number of edges along side 5, and every side has at least five edges.

7.title: The signature at every level, and the Daedalus Theorem
7.summary: Every composition is reached from its level-1 form by lengthening two edges at a time, which changes nothing, so the 18 level-1 compositions, computed, give every supertile the signature; a closed strand would lie inside one supertile, so a tiling whose hierarchy covers the plane has none: the Daedalus Theorem.

8.title: The nest tiling
8.summary: The nest tiling is grown from one tile, each block child 1 of the next; each block lies strictly inside the block two levels up, so the blocks cover the plane.

9.title: Merging, and the Ariadne Theorem
9.summary: The junction map, computed at level 1 and carried up by the same lengthening, puts every arc of $N_b$ on one arc of $N_{b+4}$ (of $N_{b+3}$ for $b$ even), so the ribbon pieces of the nest tiling form one strand: the Ariadne Theorem.

10.title: What is covered
10.summary: The single strand is proved for the nest tiling only; along another chain the pieces appear to form three strands, which is computed, not claimed, and tilings with faults are not covered.
